subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: Replication Crisis: When Studies Don't Reproduce
description: A short lesson to help you apply Replication Crisis: When Studies Don't Reproduce.

hook.text: In 2015, scientists tried to replicate 100 psychology studies. Only 39% produced the same results. The crisis was born.

buildup.text: Replication is science's ultimate test: if others can't reproduce your results, maybe they weren't real.

discovery.text: Causes: p-hacking, publication bias, and small sample sizes.

twist.text: The crisis doesn't mean science is broken — it means science found its own flaws. That's the method working.

climax.text: Reforms are underway: pre-registration, larger samples, open data, and publishing negative results.

punchline.text: Science catches its own mistakes. That's not a crisis — it's a feature.

quiz.question: What caused the replication crisis in psychology?
options: P-hacking, publication bias, and small sample sizes

details.summary: The replication crisis is the finding that a large proportion of published scientific studies cannot be reproduced. In psychology, only about 40% of key findings replicated in a landmark 2015 study.
details.whyItMatters: If scientific results do not replicate, the knowledge they represent may be built on sand. Understanding the crisis helps you calibrate trust in individual studies.
takeaways: A majority of studies in some fields fail to replicate
Publication bias favoring positive results is a major driver
Pre-registration and open data are solutions gaining traction

faq.question: What caused the replication crisis in scientific research?
faq.answer: Publication bias toward positive results, small sample sizes, p-hacking to find significance, and pressure to publish novel findings all contributed. The system incentivized exciting results over reliable ones.

faq.question: How should the replication crisis change how you interpret studies?
faq.answer: Be cautious about single studies, especially with small samples or surprising results. Look for replications and meta-analyses. A finding that has been reproduced multiple times by independent teams is far more reliable.
